title: Nasseconset, Sachem of the Nissequogue
summary: Nasseconset, also written in variants such as Nassaconsett, Nasseconseke, Nasseconsack, Nesconsake, and Nassaskonsuk, was a Nissequogue sachem named in mid-seventeenth-century land records around the Nissequogue River and Smithtown.
content:
Nasseconset, whose name appears in several spellings, was a Nissequogue sachem documented in land negotiations around the Nissequogue River and Smithtown in 1650 and 1664. The cited records do not establish his birth or death dates.

The surviving written record is concentrated in deed disputes and town histories, so Nasseconset is remembered here through documented negotiations rather than an invented full biography.23

Historical Context

Richard Smith contested a 1650 deed between Jonas Wood and Nasseconseke, placing Nasseconset in early land negotiations around Nissequogue territory.2

In 1664, Nasseconset settled a protracted Smithtown land dispute with Richard Smith through a quitclaim remembered in later accounts of the region.4

The connected map places are broad labels for the Nissequogue River, Smithtown, and Crab Meadow/Katawamake area, not precise markers for private or sensitive locations.13

References

  1. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent, pp. 154-155, 158-159.
  2. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700, p. 321.
  3. Records of the Town of Smithtown, Long Island, N.Y.
  4. John A. Strong, "Quashawam: Sunksquaw of the Montauk," Long Island Historical Journal, 1991, p. 199.
why_this_matters: Nasseconset connects the Nissequogue River and Smithtown area to a named Indigenous leader, while reminding visitors that deeds preserve only a narrow colonial view of Native authority.
